seo_title: In Washington there is no such thing as a civilian
seo_description: The opening entry: in Washington everyone is part of some greater plan, and after fourteen years the narrator realizes he has been a dupe and a fool.

seo_title: Working eleven years in Washington’s private sector
seo_description: The narrator introduces himself: eleven years in private sector Washington, never in government or the military, cleared only to contract for Treasury.

seo_title: Why nobody chooses to be part of the plan in Washington
seo_description: A short meditation on the plan: you are part of it whether you consent or not, only those who need to know are told, and much money goes to keeping it so.

seo_title: A security state built to keep the public from panic
seo_description: Someone in the world of intrigue tells the narrator that most military money exists to keep citizens calm, the way parents shield children from adult fears.

seo_title: Beginning to see the threads that make up the fabric
seo_description: The narrator becomes privy to the patterns, sees the threads of the fabric, and realizes his father was scared too, all part of a drunken pub crawl.

seo_title: Washington as one long drunken pub crawl from bar to bar
seo_description: The narrator explains a pub crawl, a night of moving from bar to bar that grows harder as everyone gets drunk, setting up a metaphor for life in Washington.

seo_title: Keeping a drunken pub crawl together until the last bar
seo_description: Late in a pub crawl, the only way forward is keeping every crawler together and moving, since one missing person could break the whole night apart.

seo_title: The white security blimp floating over Washington, DC
seo_description: A short entry about the new white security blimp floating over the Beltway; nobody quite knows what it does, only that it is for our security.

seo_title: A bike messenger racing packages across Washington, DC
seo_description: In college the narrator worked as a bike messenger for WEx, hustling legal and government packages across DC as the fax machine killed the trade.

seo_title: Couriers, Senate guards and searches in old Washington
seo_description: As a college student and courier, the narrator recalls how guards pulled knives and pipes from couriers’ bags, then simply let them make their delivery.

seo_title: How building security changed bike courier work in DC
seo_description: The narrator wonders how much time modern security takes from couriers, now that even office buildings control entry and walking in at will is past.

seo_title: Who in your own circle is quietly watching and reporting?
seo_description: A short entry in which the narrator wonders how intimate the security model is, and how close he is to someone keeping their eyes open on him.

seo_title: How spies are trained to work a crowd without being noticed
seo_description: A friend in the business describes his training: blending in, working a crowd, checking for unfriendlies and listening in without raising suspicion.

seo_title: A maddening year spent wondering if the patterns are real
seo_description: The narrator says the last year has been maddening, sure he has become part of something larger yet always worried about the false positives.

seo_title: In Washington nobody is truly private sector, cleared or not
seo_description: The narrator argues that the fully awake in Washington hold clearances, comparing it to submarine work where each worker sees only his own small part.

seo_title: Why submarine factory workers never knew what they built
seo_description: Workers at a Connecticut submarine plant built parts blind, a maze of secrecy meant to protect them from becoming traitors, unwitting or otherwise.

seo_title: Emergent systems: is a human being a hive of cells?
seo_description: A short essay on emergent systems and the idea that every organism is a suit of armor for its genes, built by a hit or miss process to survive.

seo_title: Have humans outsourced evolution to culture and technology?
seo_description: Some believe humans now evolve as a culture rather than a species, linked by technology, a system that needs its members present but not awake.

seo_title: How bee hives and ant colonies work without anyone in charge
seo_description: A look at emergent systems: no queen gives orders, no member knows the plan, and each ant or bee reacts only to simple local signals around it.

seo_title: Why a culture can be steered but never commanded outright
seo_description: Like bee hives and ant colonies, whole cultures can be redirected, manipulated and shaped over time, but they cannot simply be ordered to obey.

seo_title: Who plans your day? Washington and the scripted life
seo_description: The narrator notes that most of us respond to our surroundings without a script, while actors and some in Washington have their days mapped out for them.

seo_title: Washington is rife with intrigue, and you are in the play
seo_description: One day the narrator realizes how planned Washington has become, and that like it or not he is part of its intrigue, a little Passion play of its own.

seo_title: A friend flies in from Berlin looking gaunt and exhausted
seo_description: W arrives at Dulles from Berlin, looking gaunt and exhausted, and the first thing he does at the narrator’s apartment is ask to take a shower.

seo_title: A friend’s stainless dive watch that hides something inside
seo_description: While his friend W showers, the narrator handles W’s heavy dive watch and pulls the crown out on a hidden black filament, just as the bathroom door opens.

seo_title: A friend reclaims his watch without a single glance
seo_description: Back from the shower, W fastens his dive watch in one smooth motion and screws down the crown without ever once meeting the narrator’s eyes.

seo_title: Small doubts about a houseguest and the shampoo he used
seo_description: While W showers, the narrator worries over whether he left shampoo and shower gel for his guest, and whether the steam smells of soap he provided.

seo_title: A white kid starting Catholic school in Hawaii in 7th grade
seo_description: The narrator leaves public school for an all boys Catholic school in Hawaii, where he first sees army uniforms all over campus every Thursday.

seo_title: Choosing to join JROTC at a Catholic school in Hawaii
seo_description: In 9th grade the narrator faces three choices, band geek, jock or cadet, and joins the Junior Reserve Officer Training Corps at his Catholic school.

seo_title: Thursday parade drill and a rifle range at a Hawaii school
seo_description: Why JROTC cadets wore Class A uniforms on Thursdays: parade drill on the football field, wooden rifles, polished brass, and their own firing range.

seo_title: Becoming a JROTC cadet: berets, boots and ranks in Hawaii
seo_description: The narrator settles into JROTC at a Catholic boys school in Hawaii and notices the cadets who dress differently on Thursdays, in shined boots and berets.

seo_title: A JROTC Ranger in jump boots and a beret at a Hawaii school
seo_description: The narrator remembers Charlie, an older cadet who wore jump boots and a black beret on Thursdays and made the young cadets want to be Rangers.

seo_title: Leaving the school rifle team to join the Rangers club
seo_description: A one sentence entry: the narrator quickly leaves the JROTC rifle team and joins the Rangers, the secret club at the heart of his school years.

seo_title: A secret society inside a high school JROTC program
seo_description: Teenage cadets in a Hawaii JROTC program form the Rangers, a secret club bound by a code of silence that protects a secret able to end the whole program.

seo_title: A teenage secret the cadets could only share with each other
seo_description: The teenage cadets kept their secret out of fear and because no one else would ever believe them, and the intensity bound them only to one another.

seo_title: Teenage cadets hired out as OPFOR soldiers in war games
seo_description: On alternate weekends the narrator’s teenage JROTC unit was hired by the National Guard and Army Reserve to play the enemy in war games, with real weapons.

seo_title: A Cold War cover story told to teenage JROTC cadets
seo_description: The teen cadets were told they were secretly trained like Soviet Spetsnaz, a cover story built on the idea that operatives are raised from the cradle.

seo_title: A JROTC legend: a cadet left tied to a tree in the woods
seo_description: The narrator recalls a Ranger story passed down to new cadets: a boy captured in an ambush and left lashed to a tree in his underwear, riot cuffs and all.

seo_title: Drinking alone at a neighborhood bar to escape the strange
seo_description: The narrator heads to Zack’s for a burger and too many beers, drinking to get out of the apartment and out of his own head as life starts to feel too weird.

seo_title: A small dark neighborhood bar after a day of copying files
seo_description: After pulling documents onto a USB drive on his keychain, the narrator drops by Zack’s, a small dark bar, for pool, a burger and bottles of Bud.

seo_title: A situational drinker: what he drinks depends on the place
seo_description: The narrator explains that his drinks change with the place: Bud, Camels and pool at Zack’s, imports elsewhere, and always the local beer abroad.

seo_title: The chameleon who still gives himself away in small things
seo_description: For anyone paying attention, the narrator says, he still has the chameleon about him, and small things can tip people off in unfortunate ways.

seo_title: Why letting others order for you is a form of strength
seo_description: The narrator explains why he lets others choose the food, a habit from years of travel that gives him a more authentic experience of every place.

seo_title: A spidey sense: intuition that kept a traveler safe abroad
seo_description: The narrator describes an almost physical sixth sense for danger and intent, a sensitivity that kept him safe traveling the world alone as a photographer.

seo_title: Growing up haole: fighting as a white kid in Hawaii schools
seo_description: The narrator grew up as a haole, a white minority, in Hawaii schools with an unofficial kill haole day, and learned to fight and to be acknowledged.

seo_title: Street safety in the city: hands, posture and eye contact
seo_description: A big man explains his rules for walking unfamiliar streets at night: hands in pockets, walking with purpose or insouciance, and always making eye contact.

seo_title: Trained long ago to sense a tail and hide it behind a smile
seo_description: Twenty years after his training, the narrator still believes he can smell a tail or bad intent, and hide that awareness behind a mild, sweet exterior.

seo_title: How a camera gives you permission to look deeply at people
seo_description: W tells the narrator that because he looks so hard, he should stay a photographer, since photographers are allowed to look deeply and are forgiven.

seo_title: A photographer as Emerson’s invisible eye on the world
seo_description: As an only child and a photographer’s son, the narrator saw himself as an observer who never changes what he watches, like a scientist or anthropologist.

seo_title: Seeing the world without a camera and feeling exposed
seo_description: Without a camera between him and the world, the narrator feels conspicuous and vulnerable, and fears he has been an unwitting part of something nasty.

seo_title: An easy mark: nobody has died and nobody tried to kill me
seo_description: A very short entry in which the narrator takes stock of his situation, grateful that no one has died or tried to kill him, since he would be an easy mark.

seo_title: Dressing preppy in DC while running a countercultural site
seo_description: The narrator dresses as normally as possible in Washington while secretly hosting and editing one of the most countercultural websites on the Internet.

seo_title: Running a website after 9/11 and the madness it let in
seo_description: The narrator admits he cannot avoid influencing what he watches; after 9/11 the submissions to his open website grew so mad he can barely believe them.

seo_title: Memes, culture and the cost of influencing what people think
seo_description: The narrator talks about memetics: culture is easily influenced and corrupted, and unlike law, popular culture has few checks for its errors.

seo_title: Clinging to habits that hurt, like a lab rat at the chute
seo_description: The narrator sees himself returning again and again to painful, addictive behavior, like a lab rat drawn back to a vending chute that shocks it.

seo_title: Reliability beats cleverness: the ant and the grasshopper
seo_description: The narrator is no longer amused by clever; smarts and reliability earn the rewards, as the hard working ant ends up storing the grasshopper for winter.

seo_title: Why ants and big families outlive their individual members
seo_description: The narrator compares an ant colony, which lives for decades while each ant dies quickly, to the large blood family that outlasts any one of its members.

seo_title: Why big families gain power by covering every profession
seo_description: The narrator sees why big families matter: with members as doctor, lawyer, CEO, priest and banker, a family becomes a self contained power bound by blood.

seo_title: Life as abstract art: what is real once you look closely
seo_description: After thinking himself clever, the narrator wants to accept things as they seem, comparing what he has seen behind the curtain to abstract expressionism.

seo_title: Buying what you’re sold: wife, children and a quiet life
seo_description: The narrator decides to buy what he is being sold, a contained life with a wife and future children, and leave the social experiments to others.

seo_title: Wishing he had bought into a quiet, protected life earlier
seo_description: The narrator admits some bitterness: he wishes he were less clever and had bought into the protected, ordinary life years earlier, babies and all.

seo_title: What intelligence work is really for: preventing panic
seo_description: The narrator wants to forget that intelligence work exists to quell unrest and prevent panic, and that the parents, the government, are scared too.

seo_title: A warning to stay asleep before life becomes an allegory
seo_description: Looking back with 20/10 hindsight, the narrator warns readers to stay asleep: once you push on the other, it pushes back, and he conned his way in too far.

seo_title: An old friend whose watercolors cover the narrator’s walls
seo_description: A two line entry about L, a friend of more than five years whose watercolors hang all over the narrator’s apartment, and who is quite talented.

seo_title: The night on acid when a friend hinted at his secret life
seo_description: On the National Mall, at the strange start of an acid trip, the narrator’s friend W lets him in on a secret he would not understand for nearly ten years.

seo_title: Why staring at strangers looks suspicious without a camera
seo_description: W explains why looking hard at people is threatening unless you carry a camera, notebook or sketch pad, the props that give a watcher permission to look.

seo_title: Pattern recognition: why a man alone on a bench looks odd
seo_description: On a cold bench W explains that sitting alone without a newspaper looks threatening, because people recognize patterns and notice anything off.

seo_title: Why a man watching a playground alone seems like a threat
seo_description: W explains that a grown man watching children at a park without a child of his own reads as a pervert or kidnapper, to parents and police alike.

seo_title: Hiding in plain sight: dress and act like everyone else
seo_description: W tells the narrator that blending in is more than clothes; it is about choices that never set off an alarm, because the best hiding place is plain sight.

seo_title: Everything is exactly the opposite of how it looks
seo_description: A lesson the narrator lost and found again: everything is hidden in plain sight, and the real power in an organization often sits at the bottom of the chart.

seo_title: How many partners his partners have had, and what they count
seo_description: The narrator reflects on discovering that most women he dated had more partners than he expected, and that some encounters were never counted at all.

seo_title: Friends urge therapy as the narrator feels himself change
seo_description: Friends suggest a therapist and his mother asks about his old medication; the narrator admits he has not been himself lately and is changing fast.

seo_title: Huxley’s reducing valve: why successful people filter more
seo_description: Drawing on Aldous Huxley’s Doors of Perception, the narrator argues the brain is a reducing valve and the most successful people filter the most.

seo_title: Training the brain to filter out what it notices too well
seo_description: The narrator wants to strengthen his mind’s filter against the static he notices, a talent for patterns that began as curiosity and became a burden.

seo_title: Wanting to bumble around like a regular, unwatched man
seo_description: A very short entry about the narrator’s longing to stop noticing patterns and simply bumble through life like an ordinary person in the sentient world.

seo_title: The mind as a filter and projector of the world we see
seo_description: The narrator believes the world we sense is illusory: we see swirling balls of energy and light, and our minds project familiar patterns onto them.

seo_title: A soldier home from Iraq who must travel under another name
seo_description: A friend returning from Iraq could not visit friends in Europe because his military ID and passport carried a different name and a full cover story.

seo_title: Living under a false name: operators who can’t see friends
seo_description: Men on covert work carry fully legal papers in another name; a friend explains why he couldn’t visit a friend in Brussels while he was traveling as J.

seo_title: Lonely spies drinking in an Alexandria basement dive bar
seo_description: In a basement bar off King Street, a friend explains that intelligence people drink there, lonely and full of secrets: nobody knows your successes.

seo_title: The lonely lives of people who keep the nation’s secrets
seo_description: Intelligence men and women, full of pride and hunger, carry vows of secrecy and the world on their shoulders, as lonely as the narrator but with better stories.

seo_title: Why elite operators can’t ask for help with stress or PTSD
seo_description: A friend explains the catch: elite operators who seek therapy for stress or depression are labeled broken, so they keep their hurt to themselves.

seo_title: Lap dances at roadside strip bars and the simulacrum of sex
seo_description: The narrator visits roadside strip bars full of truckers and salesmen and realizes a lap dance sells a simulacrum of sex, a memory of a better woman.

seo_title: When the idea of a thing becomes as real as the thing
seo_description: A short reflection: the suggestion of the thing is the thing, and saying you once owned a Triumph sports car is as meaningless, and as real, as owning one.

seo_title: British empire versus American empire: husband or baby daddy
seo_description: The narrator compares empires: Britain treated colonies as brides and left bitter ex wives, while America is the world’s baby daddy, not its husband.

seo_title: How powerful influence changes a culture without being seen
seo_description: The narrator explains why real influence goes unnoticed: it rewrites institutional memory, so you must log and audit a system before the influence begins.

seo_title: Crewing a sailboat from Acapulco to Marina del Rey
seo_description: A city dweller who grew up diving in Hawaii recalls crewing a working sailboat for months from Acapulco to Marina del Rey with W and one other man.

seo_title: Lessons from the sea: gentle on the surface, life or death
seo_description: Sailing teaches hard lessons: the sea protects fools and drunks, but push past your limits and you will be hurt; she seems gentle, yet it is life or death.

seo_title: Target acquisition: how trained eyes spot distant movement
seo_description: In training the narrator learned that to defend a perimeter you stare at nothing in particular, so the slightest movement breaks the pattern and draws the eye.

seo_title: Silent movement training: moving through a forest unheard
seo_description: The narrator recalls silent movement drills in BDUs and jungle boots, jumping in place to find rattling gear, then avoiding the enemy’s pattern recognition.

seo_title: Blindfolded stalking drills straight out of a kung fu movie
seo_description: The narrator describes training where a blindfolded team leader dared cadets to sneak past: crouched, loose limbed, toeing forward like in a minefield.

seo_title: Walking home alone at night with your guard up and alert
seo_description: Walking home late, the narrator stays alert to anyone closing in, and explains how he double backs, ducks into alleys or follows a follower.

seo_title: When your own story sounds insane when you say it out loud
seo_description: A one line entry in which the narrator admits that everything he has been describing about spies, patterns and the plan sounds insane to say out loud.

seo_title: Why a painter at an easel has the perfect cover for a spy
seo_description: W says if you are going to stare you need an excuse, and a painter on Capitol Hill has the best one: hours at an easel watching anything or anyone.

seo_title: How to spot a watcher pretending to read in a coffee shop
seo_description: A man at Starbucks checks out interns from behind small shades and a French magazine; the narrator’s lesson is simple: never turn your head.

seo_title: Seduction, propaganda and why people prefer a pleasant lie
seo_description: Quoting his fairy godmother, the narrator says nothing is as frightening as a panicked public, and like seduction, influence works best when it feels good.

seo_title: Why so many backpackers are jailed abroad as spies
seo_description: The narrator argues that tourists and backpackers get harassed by foreign powers because spies really do dress like them to avoid detection.

seo_title: Why spies dress like tourists and backpackers abroad
seo_description: Operatives dress like eco tourists and backpackers for practical reasons: jungle boots, day packs and guidebooks, and tourists now outfit like soldiers.

seo_title: The real spy is the dull, average man sitting next to you
seo_description: Unlike Hollywood spies, the real field officer is Joe Average: average height and weight, dark hair, unnoticed on the metro, and highly trained.

seo_title: Real operators are average height, not action heroes
seo_description: The tall narrator notes that his friends known to be trained killers are of average build, the kind who share jeans, yet can carry or beat him easily.

seo_title: How to spot a spy: watch him at the bar after a few drinks
seo_description: The narrator’s theory of bar spies: an average looking man who drinks without fear and is very popular with women, without obvious wealth, may be a spy.

seo_title: The pecking order among cops, soldiers, spies and mercs
seo_description: Cops dislike private eyes, soldiers hate mercenaries, and government spies resent private intelligence firms, a rivalry of duty against cash.

seo_title: Why so many spies grew up wanting to be James Bond
seo_description: The narrator claims nearly every American intelligence officer keeps a shelf of spy novels at home, and that every one wanted to be James Bond growing up.

seo_title: Two friends competing to become James Bond since college
seo_description: The narrator and his best friend W have competed since college to gain the most James Bond skills, from languages to guerrilla warfare training.

seo_title: Cover, concealment and camouflage: the art of hiding secrets
seo_description: The narrator argues that camouflage, hiding in plain sight, is underrated, because the mind cannot search for what it does not recognize as a pattern.

seo_title: Camouflage, moles and the hidden secrets of Freemasonry
seo_description: Why not hide everything with camouflage? Because spycraft is built to find patterns, yet hiding in plain sight, as in Freemasonry, is still most secure.

title_starts: The Most Important Skill in Hunting
seo_title: The most important skill in hunting: waiting for the shot
seo_description: After the rifle, the guide, the training and the license, the narrator says a hunt is nothing without the patience to wait for the perfect, clear kill.

seo_title: The most important skill for a sniper is patience to wait
seo_description: After the rifle, the camouflage, the training and the drop zone, a sniper’s mission is nothing without the patience to wait for the perfect, clear kill.

title_starts: The Most Important Skill in Spying
seo_title: The most important skill for a mole in place is patience
seo_description: After the clearance, cover and reputation, a mole is nothing without the patience to wait for the perfect opportunity, which knocks only once.

seo_title: The Capitol Hill uniform: khakis, blue blazer, penny loafers
seo_description: The narrator describes Washington camouflage: khakis, a blue button down, penny loafers and a blue blazer, whether from the Gap or from Brooks Brothers.

seo_title: Why keep writing about all of this? A moment of doubt
seo_description: A one sentence entry in which the narrator admits he doesn’t really know why he keeps going on and on about spies, patterns and all of this stuff.

seo_title: Don’t I know you? The question every deep cover agent fears
seo_description: Every deep cover operative fears being recognized from a previous life; the Soviets raised moles from the cradle, while the West recruits mid career.

seo_title: Be discreet in all things: Wellington on staying unnoticed
seo_description: Quoting the Duke of Wellington, the narrator argues that if it seems impossible you hold anything valuable, you are safe; mystery gets a mole killed.

seo_title: Old women as informers: the babushkas of the Soviet Union
seo_description: The narrator notes that babushkas made the best informers in the Soviet Union, because the old, the fat and the ugly are invisible yet everywhere.

seo_title: Spy technology runs thirty years ahead of what we see
seo_description: Spy satellites read license plates in the 1970s, the narrator argues, so keeping secrets today is less about better locks than leaving no target at all.

seo_title: Choosing the true cup: the art of telling real from fake
seo_description: Like Indiana Jones choosing the true grail among a hundred poisoned cups, the narrator says recognizing the real message among the false is a rare art.

seo_title: Why doctors make ideal spy recruits through extortion
seo_description: The narrator argues doctors are the best recruits in spycraft: rich, time poor, compartmentalized, and vulnerable to extortion over private indiscretions.

seo_title: Talked down from a panic attack: nothing there there, yet
seo_description: A man tells the hyperventilating narrator to stop struggling: nobody will know unless he tells, he hasn’t done anything yet, and his mind is looping.

seo_title: A panic attack, a brown paper bag, and a cruel warning
seo_description: During a panic attack the narrator breathes into an onion scented paper sack while a calm, cruel acquaintance tells him it is a really bad sign.

seo_title: Waking in dread from a dream that leaves a wet pillow
seo_description: The narrator wakes with sweaty hair and a wet pillow from a dream he can’t recall, and wonders if the dread behind his nerves is locked inside it.

seo_title: Sousveillance: watching the watchers in a crowd of strangers
seo_description: The narrator feels he is observing the observers, spotting listening posts and surveillers in crowds, and asks if that makes him a sousveiller.

seo_title: Always assume you’re being hustled by the simple man
seo_description: A short rule of thumb: listen hard when someone opens with I’m just a simple man and I don’t know much, because you are probably being hustled.

seo_title: Charm is never incidental: follow the attention, not money
seo_description: Charm costs time and energy, so watch who is spending it and on whom; following someone’s attention can reveal more than following their money.

seo_title: Struggle or play dead: escaping when held underwater
seo_description: From quicksand to being held underwater, the narrator advises against struggling: going limp saves strength and may create one chance to escape.

seo_title: Affairs as control: secret lovers and a life of obligation
seo_description: When he feels he has lost control, the narrator seeks lovers, and describes how keeping his own secrets makes him feel like his own master again.

seo_title: The star nosed mole and why it appears in the banner
seo_description: The narrator explains why he identifies with the star nosed mole, Condylura cristata, quoting a field description of its habitat, star nose and habits.

seo_title: Moles who wait a lifetime for a call that never comes
seo_description: Moles spend their lives waiting for the other shoe to drop, often forgetting what they are, with one handler, no paper trail, and no one to believe them.

seo_title: The Mata Hari syndrome: sex as an intelligence vulnerability
seo_description: Analysts must report time spent with foreign nationals, but hookups, escorts and affairs go unreported, a gap that has long been a boon to spycraft.

seo_title: Spying on your spouse: why everyone has already done it
seo_description: Halfway through his thirties, the narrator notes that people in love snoop on each other constantly, from rifling through bags to reading private messages.

seo_title: A life so full of coincidence it seems manufactured
seo_description: The narrator says his life is full of serendipity and coincidence that he no longer believes are accidental, which is why it sounds so implausible.

seo_title: Langley kids who grew up knowing not to talk about the CIA
seo_description: A friend raised in McLean, Virginia, near CIA headquarters, recalls that every kid knew whose dad was CIA and knew never to talk about it with anyone.

seo_title: Despite Poe, secrets are kept successfully every day
seo_description: Despite what Poe said about guilty conscience, the narrator notes, families keep skeletons in their closets for generations without any oath.

seo_title: The iPod as a listening device in the age of camera phones
seo_description: In 2006, the narrator considers how camera phones, BlackBerrys and video iPods could capture intelligence or be rewired to hide bugs and GPS.

seo_title: Why the best spy is an introvert, like a method actor
seo_description: The narrator compares spycraft to acting: both need deep, unbroken character work, and the best performers, like the best spies, are quiet introverts.

seo_title: Toppling governments and souls with the seven deadly sins
seo_description: The narrator argues the surest way to destroy a person or government is through the seven deadly sins, and offers a short refresher on each of the seven.

seo_title: Why patience beats action: good things come to the patient
seo_description: After years of fighting, the narrator values patience: timing, good intelligence and a plan B, because you cannot be ambushed if you are not there.

seo_title: Domestic intelligence in America has always existed
seo_description: The narrator argues that the American government has always watched its citizens, quietly, to avoid blowback, while officially denying that it does.

seo_title: Constant war and fear: Orwell on endless war and safety
seo_description: Quoting Orwell, the narrator argues that continuous war, crime or terror breeds the fear and insecurity that lead people to give up privacy.

seo_title: Washington before 9/11 security: a courier racing the clock
seo_description: As a DC bike courier before the Internet, the narrator raced lawyers’ filings to official time stamp machines across a city that was still wide open.

seo_title: When Capitol Hill was open: a bike courier before 9/11
seo_description: A DC courier recalls moving freely between the Capitol and the Senate and House office buildings, grabbing lunch in the Capitol cafeteria in summer.

seo_title: It takes two to keep an affair or one night stand discreet
seo_description: The narrator advises that a secret affair is never secret if either partner brags or confides, and that infidelity makes you a liar and a target.

seo_title: Why cheating is so hard to keep secret under scrutiny
seo_description: Cheating means hiding from someone who knows you well, and once you are under scrutiny, human nature makes keeping the story straight nearly impossible.

seo_title: How to cheat on a spouse: a spy’s rules of total discretion
seo_description: Written in a spy’s voice, the narrator lists the conditions for an affair to stay secret, warning that the weakest link is always the lover.

seo_title: Why covert operatives should stay home on New Year’s Eve
seo_description: Drink and sentiment on New Year’s Eve can push a hardened operative to confess his double life to someone he loves, which can get him killed.

seo_title: Where business intelligence and spycraft meet in PR
seo_description: The narrator, who runs a virtual PR firm, explains how online intelligence and operations work can sound like spycraft in a city full of spies.

seo_title: Public relations as Newspeak for propaganda: Edward Bernays
seo_description: The narrator traces how propaganda became a dirty word after World War Two and was replaced by public relations, a term popularized by Edward Bernays.

seo_title: Moving from Washington to Berlin after things fell apart
seo_description: Feeling cornered in Washington, the narrator sublets an apartment in Berlin arranged by his friend W, and finds himself beholden to him for it.

seo_title: How well do you really know someone? Trust and perception
seo_description: Most of what we know about people comes from what we are told and partly from experience, the narrator notes, and our minds fill in the rest.

seo_title: Why spies are hard to make in poor, multicultural Berlin
seo_description: Berlin’s diversity and unemployment make it hard to spot patterns, the narrator argues, unlike routine bound Washington, where everyone is easy to read.

seo_title: How many spies are there in America? More than you think
seo_description: Counting FBI agents, CIA officers and others in the DIA, NSA, NRO and JSOC, the narrator estimates there may be fifty thousand operators in America.

seo_title: Real spies are more couch potato than daring action hero
seo_description: The narrator notes that most spy work is sedentary, so agents now train like amateur athletes, trading cigars and scotch for marathons and races.

seo_title: Beware the simple man: why being underestimated is power
seo_description: The biggest advantage anyone can have is being underestimated, the narrator warns, so beware the modest man who says he is simple, especially in politics.

seo_title: How covert operators wear down: the psyche as weakest link
seo_description: No matter how complete the training, the narrator argues, the psyche is the weakest link in covert work, and testing a person’s mettle is an art.

seo_title: Why gifted, isolated students make the best hidden spies
seo_description: The narrator argues that bright students who felt isolated and rejected make the best spies by accident, ripe for service and almost impossible to spot.

seo_title: Bribery, blackmail and coercion: secrets make you a target
seo_description: If you would be ashamed for family to learn something, the narrator warns, you can be blackmailed, which is why security clearances focus on lies.

seo_title: How spies are really recruited: online applications, tests
seo_description: Unlike the movies, the narrator says, spies apply online, take tests at home, then wait in rooms near Dulles after leaving their phones in the car.

seo_title: Panic, propaganda and friends losing their minds in 2017
seo_description: The narrator watches smart friends lose their composure over media reports and tweets, as vulnerable to propaganda as audiences were in the 1980s.

seo_title: Flying to Kathmandu during Desert Storm on a bargain charter
seo_description: The narrator recalls flying over the Soviet Union to Kathmandu on a cheap charter in the first days of Desert Storm, past fields of dead aircraft.

seo_title: Loneliness kills middle aged men as surely as heart disease
seo_description: The narrator reflects on how loneliness harms middle aged men even within families, and how friendship takes only modest effort and proximity.

seo_title: Sharpshooting and eyesight: why great shooters wear glasses
seo_description: The narrator notes that many of the best shooters he knows wear thick glasses, and describes his own pistol focus on the front sight, not the target.

seo_title: How intelligence agencies assign false names to field agents
seo_description: The narrator says the CIA assigns aliases that agents keep for life, while defense intelligence lets operatives choose their own names and stories.

seo_title: The perfect spy looks average: height, build and IQ
seo_description: An ideal field operative, the narrator says, is average in height, weight and looks, bright but forgettable, with a natural cloak of invisibility.

seo_title: Am I anyone of note? Wondering if I was ever recruited
seo_description: After years of hints, the narrator wonders if he was ever tapped or kept on reserve, though he has no handler, no number stations and no evidence.

seo_title: Police use of force: why officers shoot center mass
seo_description: The narrator argues that American police are trained to fire into center mass until a threat is neutralized, never to wing or wound a suspect.

seo_title: A concealed carry permit as a conditional license to kill
seo_description: The narrator describes his Virginia concealed carry permit and training, arguing that it amounts in practice to a conditional double O license to kill.

seo_title: Concealed carry discretion and the problem of printing
seo_description: The narrator’s instructor stressed that a carry permit is a promise of total discretion, and explained printing, when a gun shows through clothes.

seo_title: Which holsters concealed carriers really use, and why
seo_description: Few people use shoulder holsters like on Miami Vice, the narrator notes; most choose inside the waistband holsters made of leather or Kydex.

seo_title: When you may legally draw a firearm in self defense
seo_description: The narrator explains what his instructor taught: never brandish or threaten, but drawing and firing is allowed if you truly fear for your life.

seo_title: As many shots as required but not one more in self defense
seo_description: The narrator relays what concealed carry training teaches: shoot only center mass, keep firing until the threat has stopped, then stop at once.

seo_title: The 21 foot rule and when a carrier may legally shoot
seo_description: The narrator describes the 21 foot rule from his carry training and the situations, from muggings to assaults, where lethal force may be legal.

seo_title: If you shoot someone, kill them: carry culture advice online
seo_description: The narrator reports what online carry forums teach about center mass and lawsuits, and argues the real goal is stopping an attack, not killing.

seo_title: Why a head shot is legally indefensible in self defense
seo_description: The narrator’s instructor taught center mass because a head shot or finishing shot looks like an execution and can turn self defense into murder.

seo_title: Never telegraph that you are carrying a concealed firearm
seo_description: Concealed carry trainers teach never to warn an attacker you are armed, the narrator writes, because an attacker who knows may take the gun away.

seo_title: Fire superiority: why hesitating with a pistol is dangerous
seo_description: A drawn pistol gives only a moment of fire superiority, the narrator writes, and fear, indecision or hesitation can let an attacker take it away.

seo_title: Why lawyers say never film yourself defending your home
seo_description: Online gun lawyers advise against filming a home defense shooting, the narrator writes, because the footage can look premeditated to a jury in court.

seo_title: Fifty and still waiting: aging out of a life of adventure
seo_description: Past fifty, the narrator reflects that once in you are never really out, as long as you are useful, and wonders if he is still useful at all.

seo_title: The Smith Mundt Act and domestic propaganda in America
seo_description: The narrator argues that the 2012 Smith Mundt Modernization Act gutted a law against government propaganda aimed at Americans, with big consequences.

seo_title: False equivalence: a logical fallacy or a rhetorical weapon?
seo_description: The narrator looks at the definition of false equivalence and asks who owns the phrase, and whether it is used to shut down fair comparisons.

seo_title: Apples to apples: when false equivalence isn’t false
seo_description: The narrator argues that most charges of false equivalence compare varieties of the same thing, like two kinds of apples, not apples to oranges.

seo_title: Revealing true colors: true believers versus rhetoricians
seo_description: Using a line from The Princess Bride, the narrator asks whether people who cry false equivalence are true believers or skilled debaters using a phrase.

seo_title: Godwin’s rule of Trump analogies and conversation enders
seo_description: The narrator examines comments meant to end debate in one blow, such as comparisons to Hitler and whataboutism, and why they are so very common.

seo_title: Raised on Carl Sagan and God: an oddball’s worldview
seo_description: The narrator describes growing up in Hawaii loving science, Cosmos and Einstein while believing in God, with no conflict between the two worlds.

seo_title: Why shaming people only drives their views underground
seo_description: The narrator argues that shame and humiliation never win hearts and minds; they only push beliefs out of sight, where they keep growing quietly.

seo_title: The shy Trump factor and hidden voters in the 2020 election
seo_description: Writing in 2020, the narrator compares the shy Tory factor in British polling to hidden Trump voters, predicting they would sway the election.

seo_title: Was Trump really an authoritarian autocrat? A 2020 view
seo_description: Writing before the 2020 election, the narrator argues that predictions of a Trump dictatorship had not come true and could backfire on Democrats.

seo_title: Blowback: the unintended consequences of doing good
seo_description: The narrator takes the intelligence term blowback and applies it to progress, development and good intentions, where every change has a cost.

seo_title: Manufacture of consent defined: Lippmann, Chomsky, Gramsci
seo_description: The narrator collects definitions of manufacturing consent, from Walter Lippmann in 1922 to Herman and Chomsky’s propaganda model and Gramsci.

seo_title: West coast wildfires and the idea of climate ecoterrorism
seo_description: The narrator speculates about extreme climate activists willing to cause harm now to prevent catastrophe later, framed as a provocative theory.

seo_title: COVID testing centers or distribution centers? Two theories
seo_description: The narrator questions why people were urged to visit testing centers while told to stay home, and introduces two theories, one rational, one not.

seo_title: A rational theory: COVID testing sites and contamination
seo_description: The narrator offers a theory that COVID testing centers, despite precautions, could have spread infection the way any weak link in a chain can fail.

seo_title: A conspiracy theory about COVID testing swabs, as labeled
seo_description: The narrator lays out an openly labeled conspiracy theory asking whether early testing swabs could have spread the virus faster than nature would.

seo_title: Trump’s atrocities that never came: a skeptic’s argument
seo_description: The narrator argues that feared Trump atrocities never happened and that the outrage was used to stir up 1960s style fervor among Americans.

seo_title: Afraid nobody is talking about you behind your back
seo_description: The narrator jokes that he is terrified people are not mocking him behind his back, quoting Oscar Wilde: worse than being talked about is not.

seo_title: Woken by distant Washington fireworks and fearing the worst
seo_description: Asleep five miles away, the narrator is woken by muffled Fourth of July fireworks in Washington and briefly fears something in his apartment is failing.

seo_title: President of half the country: Biden, Trump and doubt
seo_description: After Biden won, the narrator notes that half the country doubted it, just as the other half said not my president about Trump and Bush before.

seo_title: Othering: definition of a social and psychological process
seo_description: A short definition of othering, the process of attributing negative traits to other people or groups to set them apart as the opposite of us.

seo_title: The double standard: definition and a feminist critique
seo_description: A short look at double standards, applying different principles to the same situation, including Margrit Eichler’s critique of social science.

seo_title: Metanoia: the Greek word for a change of heart and mind
seo_description: A short definition of metanoia, the Greek μετάνοια, meaning after thought or beyond thought, a transformative change of heart or spiritual conversion.

seo_title: How bad was January 6th really? A skeptic’s question
seo_description: The narrator suggests the list of January 6th atrocities kept growing, and wonders if PR firms were testing how much the public would accept.

seo_title: Censoring the president: precedent and blowback in 2021
seo_description: After Trump was banned from social media, the narrator warns that every tool used to silence him is now precedent that can be used on anyone.

seo_title: Making a mountain out of a molehill: meaning and use
seo_description: A short definition of the phrase making a mountain out of a molehill: turning a small, unimportant issue into a big problem, or overreacting.

seo_title: After four years of Trump, can anyone still be shocked?
seo_description: A short sardonic entry: after four years, the narrator says, no one should have any capacity for trauma left, since nobody ended up in a gulag.

seo_title: Right wing radicalization: recruitment or seduction?
seo_description: The narrator argues that young people drift right less through recruiting than through exposure, because subversive messages feel cooler than lectures.

seo_title: A baseless novel idea: the coronavirus as a perfect crime
seo_description: The narrator sketches a premise for a novel, a deliberately baseless theory in which America releases a virus and blames China, a perfect crime.

seo_title: Our secrets are our sickness: live as if always watched
seo_description: Quoting Sartre, the narrator says privacy only exists if no one cares, so live as if spied upon, because spies use secrets as leverage against you.

seo_title: Should Fox News be boycotted out of existence? Optics matter
seo_description: The narrator distinguishes between Fox News failing in the market and being forced out, warning that the second path could make it a martyr.

seo_title: Can money undo systemic racism without public will?
seo_description: The narrator asks whether spending can end systemic racism when the will exists only among believers, and whether pressure could deepen resistance.

seo_title: With no evidence: election fraud claims and the big lie
seo_description: The narrator examines why journalists repeat with no evidence about election fraud claims, quoting Goebbels on the big lie, and a Shaggy song.

seo_title: Reparations or programs: how to address systemic racism
seo_description: The narrator argues that if America funds racial justice, direct reparations to descendants of slavery respect people more than paternalistic programs.

seo_title: Should America open its borders like the European Union?
seo_description: The narrator argues the EU is not open borders at all: it is a gated community with strict rules, and few countries to the south could meet them.

seo_title: Riots and appeasement: officials waiting out the storm
seo_description: Soldiers admit their job is killing, the narrator writes, and officials treat riots and protests the same way: wait until the energy fades and goes.

seo_title: Traffic stops and police shootings: what escalates them
seo_description: The narrator argues that people are not shot over broken taillights but over what happens after the stop: evasion, defiance and escalation by the driver.

seo_title: Going to war to save Afghan women: twenty years later
seo_description: The narrator argues that twenty years of war left Afghan widows, orphans and women suffering most, especially those branded American sympathizers.

seo_title: Ceci n’est pas une pipe: was January 6th an insurrection?
seo_description: The narrator explains why he doubts January 6th was an insurrection, noting there were no guns, and how that view isolated him among his friends.

seo_title: Don’t approach a panicking person head on: a diver’s lesson
seo_description: As a PADI divemaster, the narrator learned never to approach a panicking diver face on, a lesson he wishes he had applied to his own politics.

seo_title: Was January 6th a real coup or political theater instead?
seo_description: The narrator asks whether January 6th was a coup or high theater, arguing a coup by the most armed group in America would have involved guns.

seo_title: Germans made Hitler, Americans make Trump: leaders as signs
seo_description: The narrator argues that strongmen like Hitler or Trump are symptoms of mass feeling, filling a gap that a public creates, not the cause of it.

seo_title: Is antiracism also anti assimilation? An open question
seo_description: The narrator calls antiracism a necessary step for America, then asks whether it also rejects assimilation into a single shared American culture.

seo_title: If antiracism rejects default culture, what replaces it?
seo_description: A short follow up asking what is embraced instead if antiracism rejects the dominant culture, since that culture still governs school and work.

seo_title: Whatever happened to code switching between cultures?
seo_description: The narrator recalls when code switching, speaking the dominant culture while keeping your own, was encouraged, and asks where that idea went.

seo_title: Why people fly Trump flags: defiance and signifiers
seo_description: The narrator argues that Trump flags are now chosen to provoke, a signifier like other defiant flags, more than a statement about Trump himself.

seo_title: Trump as a harbinger of worse political conflict to come
seo_description: The narrator predicts deeper conflict whether or not Trump stays, calling him a warning of what is still coming rather than the doom itself.

seo_title: Useful idiots: meaning, Cold War origin and Lenin myth
seo_description: A useful idiot is someone who promotes a cause without grasping its goals; the narrator traces the Cold War term and the false Lenin attribution.

seo_title: The only reason to work offworld: money for family back home
seo_description: The narrator predicts space work will be like oil rigs or submarines, done for money or science, not out of any dream of colonizing the stars.

seo_title: January 6th as an American Reichstag fire: a skeptic’s view
seo_description: The narrator argues that January 6th was a weak Reichstag fire, with selfies instead of guns, and questions claims about how many people died.

seo_title: All history is subjective and written with a purpose in mind
seo_description: The narrator argues that all history is edited and written with a goal, to unite or divide a people, like the Council of Nicaea shaping a record.

seo_title: Gun ownership, homicide statistics and defunding the police
seo_description: The narrator asks what gun death statistics include and argues gun owners know guns are for defense, so talk of defunding police sells more guns.

seo_title: Berlin’s soccer hooligans and the myth of refined Germans
seo_description: After a year in Berlin, the narrator meets loutish suburban German soccer fans singing shanties on the trains, far from the cultured Germans he imagined.

seo_title: Aegrescit medendo: when the cure is worse than the disease
seo_description: An Army officer friend says Vietnam and Afghanistan were winnable only through atrocities, and the narrator applies Virgil’s line to street crime.

seo_title: Why COVID made it a terrible time to be a climate activist
seo_description: The narrator argues that the threat of dying from COVID now makes dying from climate change later a hard sell, in a country that fails marshmallow tests.

seo_title: Stop using Afghan women and girls as political props
seo_description: The narrator notes that the welfare of Afghan women became a talking point only at withdrawal, and suspects it is being used as a political gambit.

seo_title: Are you really for free speech if you would punch Nazis?
seo_description: The narrator argues that supporting free speech means defending speech you hate, and that putting justice above free speech should be admitted openly.

seo_title: Germany between fascism and antifascism: a Berlin view
seo_description: Drawing on his years in Berlin, the narrator argues that the same German trust in rules that enabled fascism now drives its fierce antifascism.

seo_title: Nazis and the woke left need each other, a relativist argues
seo_description: The narrator argues the woke left and Nazis feed on each other, and that to him any tyrant of any race or ideology can rightly be called a Nazi.

seo_title: Déjà Afghanistan: Kipling’s warning about Afghan wars
seo_description: A short entry quoting Rudyard Kipling’s lines about a wounded soldier left on Afghanistan’s plains, offered as a comment on the American withdrawal.

seo_title: Afghanistan, the graveyard of empires, and why invaders lose
seo_description: The narrator argues America invaded Afghanistan for revenge after 9/11, and Afghans endure every invader by adapting and simply waiting them out.

seo_title: Training Afghan soldiers who may fight the next invader
seo_description: The narrator suggests the 300,000 Afghan soldiers America trained were mostly learning to fight the next superpower that invades their country.

seo_title: NPR and the liberal media sound pro war on Afghanistan
seo_description: A short entry in which the narrator is gobsmacked to hear NPR correspondents sound strongly in favor of staying at war in Afghanistan in 2021.

seo_title: Darkness will engulf the world: fear as a political tool
seo_description: A short entry suggesting that for ten years leaders have used natural threats to convince people they are to blame and only experts can save them.

seo_title: How will the Taliban fly the Black Hawks left behind?
seo_description: The narrator answers that Afghan pilots trained by the US military, hired contractors, or Pakistani allies could fly the aircraft left behind.

seo_title: Afghan women, outrage, and why bombing didn’t change culture
seo_description: The narrator shares the outrage over Afghan women’s treatment but argues drones and occupation could never change a fundamentalist culture there.

seo_title: Afghanistan as a modern conquest: still saving pagan babies
seo_description: The narrator compares the American occupation of Afghanistan to Spanish conquistadors, saving souls and civilizing natives by force of arms.

seo_title: Could America have won in Afghanistan? At what moral cost?
seo_description: The narrator argues America lost because winning would have required atrocities it had no will to commit, and because it never truly moved in.

seo_title: Did Trump’s Taliban deal keep Marines alive? A question
seo_description: The narrator is confused by blaming Trump for a deal that he says protected servicemen, after thirteen died in the Kabul airport bombing in 2021.

seo_title: To tell the Afghanistan truth: who is the real Afghanistan?
seo_description: Like the game show To Tell the Truth, the narrator asks which Afghanistan is real: tribes, city intellectuals, the government, or the Taliban.

seo_title: Was Trump really like Hitler? Weighing rhetoric against acts
seo_description: The narrator argues that despite comparisons to Hitler, Trump’s term brought no death camps or pogroms, only protest, and calls the comparison weak.

seo_title: How little red America thinks about identity politics
seo_description: A one sentence entry: if blue America knew how little red America thinks about race and identity, it would be amazed, insulted and appalled.

seo_title: Did the evacuation brain drain Afghanistan of its liberals?
seo_description: The narrator asks whether evacuating pro democracy Afghans left the country without its educated reformers, leaving only fundamentalists behind.

seo_title: Too early to be grateful: loss after twenty years of war
seo_description: The narrator reflects that gratitude is hard when everything built is taken away, whether by war, disaster or the loss of someone that you love.

seo_title: Will leaving Afghanistan make terror attacks less likely?
seo_description: The narrator argues that militants may be less likely to attack America once the occupation ends, since drone strikes and bombs feed terrorism.

seo_title: Repent, sinner: 9/11, January 6th and turning the war inward
seo_description: After hearing 9/11 compared to January 6th on NPR, the narrator predicts America will turn its war on terror inward against its own rural people.

seo_title: Authoritarianism for public safety is still authoritarianism
seo_description: A thought experiment: safety is the perfect justification for authoritarian rule, since nobody wants to argue against protecting widows and orphans.

seo_title: Does anyone care about climate change enough to sacrifice?
seo_description: The narrator doubts people will make wartime sacrifices for climate, giving up travel, meat and cars, especially when the rich ignore the rules.

seo_title: When calling someone a Nazi no longer works as an insult
seo_description: The narrator notes that insults like Nazi or white supremacist no longer shame the right, and asks what comes next when insults become badges.

seo_title: Nowhere to hide: public venom from 2016 to 2021 comes back
seo_description: The narrator warns that all the public vitriol of 2016 to 2021 will be found and used against people, citing a judicial confirmation hearing.

seo_title: Yelling fire in a crowded theater: free speech and the law
seo_description: The narrator argues the familiar fire in a theater line misreads the law: rights don’t excuse crimes, but speech is not banned in advance either.

seo_title: Watching brilliant friends join online mob feeding frenzies
seo_description: The narrator describes watching some of his smartest friends get swept up in mob mentality, and finds it fascinating, troubling and maddening.

seo_title: Ivermectin is not just a horse dewormer: on trust in experts
seo_description: Without endorsing it for COVID, the narrator argues that experts who called ivermectin only a horse dewormer lost public trust by saying so.

seo_title: Facebook’s 2018 algorithm change and fears of radicalization
seo_description: The narrator asks if Facebook’s 2018 change toward friends’ posts was later called radicalization because people could no longer be filtered.

seo_title: Rising meat and fuel prices: market forces or a nudge?
seo_description: The narrator sarcastically questions whether rising meat and fuel prices are pure market forces or a nudge toward plants and away from fossil fuels.

seo_title: Legacy media versus social media: a fight over the narrative
seo_description: The narrator argues that print, radio and television are trying to protect their dominance by pushing to censor social media and online platforms.

seo_title: The progressive pendulum swings right after 2020 protests
seo_description: The narrator predicts a conservative backlash after the 2020 protests and riots, with more policing and law and order voters, not defunding.

seo_title: Is there life in the universe? Just look in the mirror
seo_description: The narrator answers the Drake equation with a joke: we are proof of life in the universe, and to believe anything else is just earthling supremacy.

seo_title: Vaccine mandates as the hill some Americans will die on
seo_description: The narrator once expected gun confiscation to spark civil conflict in America, but now thinks vaccine mandates may be the true breaking point.

seo_title: Elite contempt for rural Americans comes back at elections
seo_description: Any time an elite calls ordinary Americans rubes, the narrator warns, opposition researchers will find it and it will cost votes at election time.

seo_title: Critical race theory and the K through 12 school debate
seo_description: The narrator argues that saying Virginia schools don’t teach critical race theory sounds evasive, since CRT is a lens that shapes how history is taught.

seo_title: Using a gun against fists: self defense law in America
seo_description: The narrator explains that most American states do not require proportional force, so a gun may legally be used against an attacker using fists.

seo_title: Dear activists: your vision of the future isn’t everyone’s
seo_description: The narrator warns that constant accusations of bigotry may one day make people embrace those labels, and wonders if that has been the goal.

seo_title: Justifiable homicide: the legal definition of self defense
seo_description: The narrator quotes a legal definition of justifiable homicide: killing in reasonable fear of death or great bodily harm, or to stop a violent felony.

seo_title: How phone video redeems and damns both sides of a fight
seo_description: The narrator argues that ubiquitous phone video cuts both ways: it proves what happened, redeeming everyone’s heroes and damning everyone’s enemies.

seo_title: The state of American vigilantism in film, TV and games
seo_description: The narrator suggests Americans may not be against vigilantes at all, after a lifetime of films, books and video games that celebrate them as heroes.

seo_title: Nerds are never really cool, even as elected leaders
seo_description: The narrator compares politics to high school, where student government and grades never brought real power, and nerds grow heavy handed when ignored.

seo_title: The noble lie: Plato’s myth for keeping social harmony
seo_description: A short definition of the noble lie, a myth knowingly spread by an elite to keep social harmony or advance an agenda, from Plato’s Republic.

seo_title: The trauma wars in an immigrant nation built on suffering
seo_description: The narrator argues that in America every family carries stories of trauma, which is why so many came, making a contest of suffering hard to win.

seo_title: COVID deaths in perspective: how many Americans die daily
seo_description: The narrator puts 1,500 COVID deaths in one day beside the roughly 7,000 Americans who die every day of every year, for perspective and proportion.

seo_title: Are secret weapons really thirty years ahead? A 1986 story
seo_description: The narrator assumes real weapons run thirty years ahead, recalling an uncle at TRW who showed him particle beam weapon material back in 1986.

seo_title: How climate mitigation will really happen: a grim forecast
seo_description: The narrator predicts humans will do as little as possible about climate change, and that a slow population collapse will hit the poorest hardest.

seo_title: The Hague: why war crimes charges mean little to superpowers
seo_description: The narrator argues that an International Criminal Court accusation is almost a badge of honor, since superpowers and their allies face no enforcement.

seo_title: Is the US troop buildup in Eastern Europe a jobs program?
seo_description: A one line entry asking whether the American military buildup in Central and Eastern Europe is mainly an economic stimulus, a works program.

seo_title: Putin, Russia and a revival of Cold War The Musical
seo_description: A short satirical entry hoping Vladimir Putin is well paid for his role in a revival of Nikita Khrushchev’s Cold War, The Musical, since the first was a farce.

seo_title: Embargoes and sanctions as a road to war with Russia
seo_description: The narrator argues that sanctions on Russia echo the embargoes that pushed Japan toward Pearl Harbor, and that they can bait a country into war.

seo_title: Right speech, wrong speech and the authoritarian urge
seo_description: The narrator satirizes the idea that wrong speech must be suppressed like a disease, comparing that urge to Stalinists, Maoists and the East German Stasi.

seo_title: What Maus teaches about how every holocaust begins
seo_description: The narrator says readers of Maus learn that every holocaust begins differently and subtly, led by people you trust, like a slowly heating pot.

seo_title: Spotify, Joe Rogan and the urge to boycott and remove
seo_description: The narrator calls the boycott of Spotify over Joe Rogan mob mentality, and argues that anything labeled dangerous should be read and preserved.

seo_title: Are Americans now immune to being called racists or Nazis?
seo_description: The narrator worries that accusations of racism or Nazism have become so common that many Americans now shrug them off completely, which scares him.

seo_title: Two COVID camps in America that will never understand
seo_description: The narrator sees two camps in America: those who think COVID is the worst thing in the world and those who don’t, each side mutually appalled.

seo_title: Is Russia really the bad actor? A dissenting view from 2022
seo_description: The narrator argues that Russia has been encircled by Western bases since 2014, drawing on his trips over Russia in 1991 and to Saint Petersburg in 1996.

seo_title: Germany, Russian gas and Nord Stream before the Ukraine war
seo_description: The narrator describes Germany’s bind: it dropped coal and nuclear power, became dependent on Russian gas, and now faces a war over Ukraine.

seo_title: No dirty bomb in 72 years: was the nuclear threat staged?
seo_description: The narrator suggests that decades without a single nuclear attack or dirty bomb are suspicious, and that the threat may have been used for control.

seo_title: Not an enemy of Russia or Putin: a contrarian view in 2022
seo_description: The narrator argues Putin has been restrained and America has committed worse, and that Russia now holds Europe hostage through natural gas.

seo_title: The slave would rise in rebellion: Callicles on natural law
seo_description: A short entry quoting Callicles in Plato’s Gorgias on the strong man who throws off society’s laws and lets the light of natural justice shine.

seo_title: Consensus reality generators: TV, film and the news
seo_description: Listening to an old Art Bell show, the narrator enjoys the idea that television, film, science fiction and news work as consensus reality generators.

seo_title: These are the buds of the socialist spring: Ukraine’s famine
seo_description: A short entry quoting a passage about Ukraine’s famine, a dead mother and nursing infant at the Kharkiv market, and the bitter phrase people used.

seo_title: Are we the world? On war propaganda and liberal democracy
seo_description: The narrator calls the wave of we are the world messaging about Ukraine uncritical propaganda, and says he is against war and democracy by force.

seo_title: Vainglory: Putin, humiliation and the risk of nuclear war
seo_description: The narrator argues Putin sees NATO expansion as a broken promise, lost the moral high ground by invading Ukraine, and that humiliating him risks escalation.

seo_title: Russian or Ukrainian? Spot the source by missing articles
seo_description: The narrator jokes that you can tell messaging from Ukraine or Russia because native speakers drop English articles, so follow the articles.

seo_title: How the technology of killing has advanced since 1945
seo_description: The narrator lists how far the technology of killing has come since 1945, from nuclear weapons and drones to smart bombs and targeted biologicals.

seo_title: Dear powers that be: censorship means you’ve lost trust
seo_description: The narrator argues that relying on censorship, moderation and calling things misinformation shows leaders have lost the trust of their people.

seo_title: Free speech isn’t equitable speech: who decides who speaks?
seo_description: The narrator argues that equitable speech means someone chooses whose voice is amplified and whose is suppressed, which is power, not equality.

seo_title: Decriminalize crime: a satirical fix for the justice system
seo_description: In a satirical entry, the narrator proposes making illegal things legal so there will be fewer criminals and fewer people in jail, a glass half full view.

seo_title: Ukraine and brainwashing: who is fooled, Russia or the West?
seo_description: A short entry asking whether the Russian people, the European people, or the American people are the ones brainwashed about the war in Ukraine, or all of them.

seo_title: Populist democracy versus constitutional republic in America
seo_description: The narrator argues that the left treats America as a populist democracy while the right sees a constitutional republic where popular votes matter less.

seo_title: Sacrifice for the collective was never an American virtue
seo_description: The narrator argues America has not prized sacrifice for the collective since the 1930s, not even in World War Two, favoring isolation and greed.

seo_title: Chest seals in your go bag: who is preparing for conflict?
seo_description: Reading about the Spanish Civil War, the narrator notes that the people he knows with chest seals in their go bags are all on the political right.

seo_title: The Disinformation Governance Board: what does it mean?
seo_description: The narrator asks whether the federal Disinformation Governance Board, not called counter disinformation, produces disinformation or reduces it.

seo_title: Why gun crime always drives gun sales up in America
seo_description: The narrator notes that gun crime boosts gun sales and carry permits rather than bans, recalling stores sold out of Glock 19s after the Giffords shooting.

seo_title: Only twenty percent of Americans trust their government
seo_description: The narrator notes that with 400 million guns and only one in five Americans trusting the government in 2020, America is playing a dangerous game.

seo_title: Total retribution: Republican politics as payback over guns
seo_description: A short entry arguing that much Republican activism against Democrats is simply retribution for years of efforts to restrict guns and ammunition.

seo_title: Ashli Babbitt and the January 6th death toll narrative
seo_description: The narrator asks why accounts said five people were killed at the Capitol when the only person shot was Ashli Babbitt, and what that says about belief.

seo_title: America’s fragile democracy: whose plans are fragile?
seo_description: The narrator argues that when people say democracy is fragile, they mean their own plans are, since democracy also elects people they oppose.

seo_title: Why mass shootings drive sales of high capacity rifles
seo_description: The narrator applies Frank Luntz’s point that what people hear matters, arguing news about mass shootings makes people buy high capacity rifles.
